item.title: Math?
item.content:encoded:
(Paging Communism will win…your fix to make if you want, otherwise I'm happy to edit it.)

In the Incident Report:

…0.9 kg of it was placed on a scale…the sample of SCP-148 began to grow in mass by upwards of 50 grams per second. After one minute, this rate began to decrease, and SCP-148 ceased to increase in mass forty seconds later, at which point it weighed 1.4 kilograms.

So 900 grams, plus 50+ grams/second for 60 seconds, another 40 seconds of increase, at which point it weighs 1400 grams. Problem is that a 50 grams/second increase would hit 1400 grams in 10 seconds, and after 60 we'd have more like 4kg of the stuff than 1.4kg. This has been there since the original version so it's not an edit issue, my guess is the draft had it as 5 grams/second at some point.

Should probably either go back to 5 grams/second, or the added mass should be scaled 10x so it ends up at 5.9kg.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/extrasensory

Extrasensory does not specifically refer to the act of sensing, but here it refers to any mind-affecting properties that lie outside what is considered normal sensory intake. Like, you can affect someone's mind by rolling Persuasion against them, but so long as it occurs through the normal channels (sight, sound, fornication, etc.), Telekill won't stop that. Telekill is good against something if it:

  1. Occurs outside the realm of normal sensory things. Telepathy and ESP, regardless if this is waves going out of your mind or waves going into your mind. Not light-reflecting-off-of-things-and-into-your-eyes images.
  2. Mind-affecting. Has to affect a mind in some manner, either by giving it information or changing it. Telekinesis won't be stopped unless something is messing with something else's mind.
  3. Has to be an effect of a living organism. If you set up a computer that manipulated electromagnetic fields to fuck with people's brains, it'll go right on doing it.

What is not strictly required is that it be a mind doing it. If my liver started giving you nightmares via liverwaves (as opposed to brainwaves), Telekill would stop it. It would have no effect on your attempts to give me heart disease with your mind. It doesn't affect things based on the source, it affects things that have the ability to affect the mind.

Plus I don't feel that 'psychic' is a particularly clinical term :P

There are certain old things that don't get brought up much any more; PRI (Psionic Resistance Index) or some such being one of them. Telekill overtook them, but fell out of fashion for the same reason 682 references did: overuse. Suddenly everything was psychic that needed the magic metal to fix. even things that WEREN'T psychic were being shielded by 148 alloy because… Science?

Since the overarching canon and refined standards have been put up, cross-SCP usage is being thoroughly discouraged, and the use of 148 as such is pretty much verboten. About the only time you'll see it used is during a tale when the "Oh Shit Button" has already been pressed.

Beyond that, within a limited range of stuff it's up to the authors of individual things to come up with ways around psychic effects.

item.title: Re: What do?
item.content:encoded:
Here's a rough idea of a plan:

First, you'll need to gather all references to SCP-148 or Telekill on the wiki (it may help to create a new page to track these). Then, sort all of the references into separate piles: articles that don't need changing, humorous addenda, useless crosstests, articles that will need special attention— whatever works for you. I would think that those middle piles would essentially boil down to "yep, these are stupid and can go" once a mod gives the go ahead.

The rest, though, would probably have to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. Then, depending on whether the original author is accessible, staff can come to a consensus on how to deal with each one. But first things first— we need to know just how big an undertaking this is going to be.

item.title: What do?
item.content:encoded:
Okay, I want to remove the Telekill crosslinks from the articles that I don't feel they make sense in. They're dated, unnecessary, and the excuse that the containment procedures were written prior to finding out Telekill's side effects is just that: an excuse, not a solution. Mostly, though, they just bug me. In addition, a number of the articles are ones that I don't like, and I don't want any of my stuff to be associated with them.

Bland's list up there lists pretty much all of them, with some exceptions that I don't feel like finding at the moment. The Joke SCPs can keep them (because they're jokes and don't need to take things seriously), the archived ones can (because they're supposed to be outdated), SCP-035 can (because I feel it genuinely adds to the article and can be excused), the Olympia project can (because running it through 914 sorta makes sense still), and 914's logs can (same reason).

If this was just a single crosslink that I didn't like, I'd post in its thread and ask the author to remove it. However, I feel it's different with Telekill for these reasons:

  1. I am not Telekill's original author. This may or may not just be semantics, but in my mind I cannot claim the idea as my own entirely, and thus feel that I don't have unilateral power to edit them out. I would feel the same way with SCP-066 if something linked to it that I didn't like.
  2. The scope of the changes. There are a lot of things that would be edited. This just means that it's more work, but this places it out of the "minor fix" realm and into the "reasonably sized undertaking" category, which I may or may not have the authority to initiate.
  3. What to fill in Telekill's absence with. This isn't a problem for those that go "LOL this does/doesn't work with 148", but some use it in the containment procedures. Should the SCP be moved to a larger room? Should staff be given some other form of protection? This isn't up for me to decide. In the event that I get permission to remove the links, I'm not allowed to decide what the author does to make up for its loss. If it was a bad crosslink to begin with, the author would be rightfully obligated to do the legwork of fixing it. However…
  4. A small number of the references made sense at the time, and those authors are needed to make this work. As much as I'd like to deny it, the old Telekill was very useful, and for most of the older references the authors were doing nothing wrong by putting it in. To me, it feels unfair to make them do more work because the thing they were referencing changed right under their noses through no fault of their own.

It's entirely possible that I've blown this out of proportion and that I'm worrying too much. However, making this post seemed more prudent than making a bunch of edits without permission and getting yelled at later.

My point is, and I think most of you agree, the crosslinks to SCP-148 should go, but there are some complications to removing them. I'd really like to see this happen, so I defer to the administation and to the community: How do I go about fixing articles that link to SCP-148?
